name: Strategy & Positioning
description: Vocabulary from and around the reading list: Positioning, Obviously Awesome, Good Strategy Bad Strategy, High Growth Handbook, The Mom Test.

entries.definition: The irreducible core of a strategy: a diagnosis of the situation, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and a coherent set of actions that follow.
examples: Our Q4 kernel fits in three sentences: creators out-convert paid, so we fund the roster and starve the auction, which means the ad budget moves to retainers.
If the strategy doc has no kernel, it's a budget request with adjectives.
Rumelt's point is that most “strategies” are goals — a kernel is what turns a goal into a strategy.
conversation: Jae: Give me the strategy in three sentences.
You: That is the kernel. Creators out-convert paid, so we fund the roster and starve the auction, which means the ad budget moves to retainers.
entries.note: From Good Strategy Bad Strategy. The fastest test of any plan: can you state its diagnosis, its guiding policy, and the actions — without using the word “growth” as a verb?

entries.definition: A judgment about what is actually going on — naming the one or two things that explain the mess.
examples: My diagnosis isn't “we need more content,” it's “we have distribution and no second act — 40M views land on an onboarding built for search traffic.”
Skipping the diagnosis is why so many roadmaps are a list of everyone's favorite project.
A good diagnosis simplifies; it tells you what to ignore.
conversation: Jae: What do you think is really going on?
You: My diagnosis is not that we need more content. We have distribution and no second act.
entries.note: The first and most-skipped part of the kernel. Write the diagnosis before the plan, and half the plan writes itself.

entries.definition: The overall approach chosen to deal with the diagnosis — a direction that rules some options out.
examples: Guiding policy for the half: win on trust, not on reach. That's why we're paying retainers instead of buying impressions.
A guiding policy that forbids nothing isn't a policy, it's a slogan.
The test of a guiding policy is whether a new hire could use it to say no to something.
conversation: New hire: How do I know what to say no to?
You: The guiding policy this half is win on trust, not reach. If a tactic only buys reach, it is a no.
entries.note: Rumelt's middle term. Its whole value is exclusion — if every good idea still passes, you haven't chosen anything.

entries.definition: Fitting together so the parts reinforce each other instead of pulling in different directions.
examples: Paying creators for reach while telling them to optimize for comments isn't coherent, and they can feel the contradiction.
Five coherent actions beat fifteen good ones that don't compound.
Coherence is what makes a small budget feel like a strategy and a large one feel like a strategy.
conversation: Creator: You pay me for views but grade me on comments.
You: That is not coherent, and it is on us. From next month it is one metric.
entries.note: Rumelt's “coherent action” is the third leg of the kernel. Incoherence usually shows up as teams working hard against each other with no one at fault.

entries.definition: Close enough to be reachable — an objective near enough that the team can actually see how to hit it.
examples: Set a proximate objective: 10 creators producing 4 videos a month at under $2 CPM. “Own creator finance” is a wish, not a target.
The proximate cause was the algorithm change; the real cause was depending on one platform.
Good leadership converts a distant ambition into a proximate objective the team believes is doable.
conversation: Jae: The goal is to own creator finance.
You: That is an ambition. The proximate objective is ten creators shipping four videos a month under a two dollar CPM.
entries.note: Two senses worth keeping straight — proximate objective (near enough to attack) and proximate cause (the last domino, not the first). Both come up in postmortems.

entries.definition: A narrow initial entry point into a market — deliberately small, chosen because it can widen later.
examples: Bloom's wedge isn't “investing app” — it's “the app your favorite creator taught you to invest with.”
A wedge should be embarrassingly narrow; if it sounds like a whole market, it's not a wedge.
The wedge wins the beachhead; the roadmap decides whether it widens.
conversation: Investor: So you are an investing app.
You: That is the category. The wedge is narrower — we are the app your favourite creator taught you to invest with.
entries.note: The wedge is about entry, the moat about defense, the beachhead about the territory itself. Mixing them up muddles a positioning memo fast.

entries.definition: The first segment you take and hold completely, chosen because it makes the next segment easier.
examples: Our beachhead is 19–24 year olds who already follow finance creators — small, winnable, and adjacent to everyone we want next.
A beachhead you can't dominate isn't a beachhead, it's a pilot.
Pick the beachhead for what it opens up, not for how big it is.
conversation: Jae: Who are we actually for, this year?
You: The beachhead is nineteen to twenty-four year olds who already follow finance creators. Small, winnable, next to everyone else we want.
entries.note: From Crossing the Chasm, and the military metaphor is doing real work: the point is total control of a small area, not partial presence in a large one.

entries.definition: A structural advantage that makes a business hard to attack — something a competitor can't just buy or copy.
examples: Our moat is the roster relationship: a competitor can outbid us on any single creator and still can't replicate 40 of them at once.
Content isn't a moat. A content system with exclusive talent might be.
Every claimed moat should come with a sentence describing how a funded rival would try to cross it.
conversation: Investor: What is the moat?
You: Not the content. Forty creator relationships. You can outbid us on any one of them and still not replicate forty.
entries.note: The stress test: if a well-funded competitor showed up tomorrow with your playbook, what would still be hard? That answer is the moat; everything else is a head start.

entries.definition: The established player currently holding the position you want.
examples: The incumbent here isn't another app, it's a group chat where three friends tell each other what to buy.
Incumbents rarely lose on features; they lose on distribution changes they refuse to take seriously.
Every incumbent's advantage is also a commitment it can't easily walk away from.
conversation: Dan: Which competitor worries you?
You: None of them. The incumbent is a group chat where three friends tell each other what to buy.
entries.note: The most useful positioning question in The Mom Test register: what is the customer doing today instead? That's your real incumbent, and it's usually not a company.

entries.definition: The challenger attacking an established position, usually with fewer resources and a different shape.
examples: We're the insurgent here, which means we win on speed and specificity, not on feature count.
Insurgents pick fights incumbents can't answer without damaging their own business.
The moment an insurgent starts defending, it has to become a different company.
conversation: Jae: Should we be matching their feature list?
You: We are the insurgent. We win on speed and specificity, not on parity.
entries.note: Deciding which one you are settles a surprising number of arguments — insurgents should be picking fights, incumbents should be closing gaps.

entries.definition: The mental box a customer files you into, which sets the expectations and comparisons you're judged against.
examples: If we land in the “trading app” category we're compared on fees; in the “learn to invest” category we're compared on whether people understand anything.
Choosing the category is the highest-leverage decision in positioning, and most teams let the market choose it for them.
You don't get to be uncategorized — customers will file you somewhere within seconds.
conversation: Maya: Why does the landing page matter that much?
You: It picks the category. Land as a trading app and we get compared on fees. Land as learn-to-invest and we get compared on whether anyone understood anything.
entries.note: April Dunford's core move: the category sets the frame of reference, which sets what counts as a strength. Pick the frame where your differentiators matter.

entries.definition: The deliberate choice of what you are, who you're for, and what you're better at — the context that makes your strengths legible.
examples: Our positioning problem isn't the copy — it's that we've never decided whether we're a learning product with a brokerage or a brokerage with lessons.
Positioning happens whether you do it or not; the only question is who does it, you or the market.
Weak positioning shows up as a sales cycle where you keep explaining what you're not.
conversation: Jae: Sales says the messaging is not landing.
You: It is not a copy problem. It is positioning. We have never decided if we are a learning product with a brokerage or the reverse.
entries.note: Ries and Trout's original claim still holds: positioning is done in the customer's mind, not in your deck. You're arranging their existing furniture, not building new rooms.

entries.definition: The set of alternatives a customer mentally compares you against — the “instead of what?” behind every decision.
examples: Set the frame of reference before you list features: against a brokerage we look thin, against a finance TikTok we look accountable.
The user's frame of reference for us is a creator they trust, not a competitor we track.
Change the frame of reference and the same product becomes expensive or cheap without touching the price.
conversation: Dan: Against a real brokerage we look thin.
You: Only if that is the frame of reference. Our user is comparing us to a creator they trust, not to a brokerage.
entries.note: From Obviously Awesome. Most “our messaging isn't landing” problems are frame-of-reference problems in disguise.

entries.definition: Meaningfully different in a way the customer can perceive and cares about.
examples: Being differentiated means a user could describe why we're different without reading our website — right now most couldn't.
A feature nobody else has isn't differentiated if nobody wants it; that's just unusual.
Differentiation has to be defensible and valued, or it's trivia.
conversation: Jae: Are we differentiated?
You: Test it this way — could a user say why we are different without reading our site? Right now most could not.
entries.note: Two tests: can a customer name the difference, and would they pay for it? Failing either means you're merely different, not differentiated.

entries.definition: To turn something distinctive into an interchangeable good, where price becomes the only remaining difference.
examples: AI scripting tools are commoditizing hook writing; what they can't commoditize is a creator whose audience believes her.
Once every app has fractional shares, fractional shares are commoditized and we're back to competing on trust.
Commoditize your complement — make the thing next to you cheap so the thing you sell gets more valuable.
conversation: Maya: The AI script tools are getting good.
You: They will commoditize hook writing. What they cannot commoditize is a creator whose audience believes her.
entries.note: The strategic question is always which layer is being commoditized and which is capturing the value that leaks out of it.

entries.definition: The minimum required to be considered at all — necessary to compete, useless as a differentiator.
examples: Instant transfers are table stakes now; putting them on the landing page is spending our best real estate on the price of entry.
Table stakes still have to be built — you just don't get to brag about them.
Confusing table stakes with differentiation produces marketing that sounds like every competitor's.
conversation: Dan: Should instant transfers go on the homepage?
You: They are table stakes now. That is our best real estate spent on the price of entry.
entries.note: Sorting features into table stakes vs. differentiators is the single most clarifying hour you can spend before a positioning rewrite.

entries.definition: Something already done by the time anyone gets to object — a decision presented as settled.
examples: Rather than pitching a Spanish-language pilot, I ran it with two creators for three weeks and brought Jae a fait accompli with numbers attached.
The platform's algorithm change was a fait accompli; the only question was how fast we adapted.
A fait accompli spends trust — worth it for small reversible bets, expensive for anything else.
conversation: Jae: You ran a Spanish pilot without asking.
You: Two creators, three weeks, my own budget line. I would rather bring you a fait accompli with numbers than a slide with a hope.
entries.note: French, kept in English because there's no clean equivalent. Powerful and slightly aggressive: use it about your own moves sparingly, and never on something hard to undo.

entries.definition: To attack from the side rather than head-on — going where the competitor isn't defending.
examples: We're not going to outspend the incumbents on app-install ads; we flank them by owning the creator's comment section, where they don't show up at all.
Flanking works because the incumbent's strength points forward.
A flanking move that the leader can copy in a week isn't a flanking move.
conversation: Jae: We cannot outspend them on install ads.
You: So we flank. We own the comment section, where they do not show up at all.
entries.note: Ries and Trout's classic move for a challenger. Pick the flank the incumbent can't defend without contradicting its own business.

entries.definition: The narrow place everything must pass through — control it and you control the flow.
examples: The chokepoint in Gen Z finance isn't the brokerage, it's the 12 creators who decide what 4 million people think is a good idea this month.
Own a chokepoint and you don't have to be the best product in the category.
Every chokepoint eventually attracts a competitor trying to route around it.
conversation: Investor: Where is the leverage in this market?
You: The chokepoint is twelve creators who decide what four million people think is a good idea this month.
entries.note: Distinct from a bottleneck: a bottleneck limits your own throughput, a chokepoint is a position of power over a market.

entries.definition: When each additional user makes the product more valuable to every other user.
examples: We don't have a network effect yet — more users don't make Bloom better for existing users, they just make our chart nicer.
The creator roster has a weak network effect: each good creator makes recruiting the next one easier.
Real network effects show up as retention that improves with cohort size, not just as growth.
conversation: Investor: Do you have network effects?
You: Not yet, honestly. More users do not make the app better for existing users. They just make the chart nicer.
entries.note: The most over-claimed advantage in startup writing. If you can't name the mechanism by which user N+1 helps user N, you have scale, not a network effect.

entries.definition: What a customer must spend — in money, effort, or lost history — to move to a competitor.
examples: Our switching costs are near zero: a user's whole relationship is with the creator, not with us, and the creator is portable.
Transferring a funded account creates a real switching cost, which is why activation matters more than installs.
Switching costs built on friction are resented; switching costs built on accumulated value are earned.
conversation: Jae: How sticky are we?
You: Switching costs are near zero. The relationship is with the creator, and the creator is portable.
entries.note: The honest way to distinguish the two: would the customer keep the accumulated thing if leaving were free? If yes, that's value. If no, it's a hostage.

entries.definition: A situation where leaving is impractical, whether or not the customer still wants to stay.
examples: I'd rather build retention than lock-in — this audience talks to each other and punishes anything that feels like a trap.
Data portability rules are eroding the lock-in that a decade of fintech was built on.
Lock-in flatters your retention numbers right up until a competitor makes leaving one tap.
conversation: Dan: Should we make transfers out harder?
You: No. Lock-in flatters retention right up until a competitor makes leaving one tap. This audience talks to each other.
entries.note: Carries a negative charge that switching cost doesn't. Say lock-in about a rival, switching cost about yourself, and know you're doing it.

entries.definition: To cut out the middle layer between two parties who could deal directly.
examples: The real risk isn't a competitor — it's a top creator disintermediating us by launching her own product to the audience we helped her monetize.
Every marketplace lives with the fear of being disintermediated by its own best users.
Platforms disintermediate agencies; creators disintermediate platforms; the cycle doesn't stop.
conversation: Jae: What actually keeps you up at night?
You: A top creator disintermediating us — launching her own product to the audience we helped her monetise.
entries.note: Long word, precise meaning, no clean substitute. The defense is always to be worth more than the fee you charge for standing in the middle.

entries.definition: A neighboring market or use case you can reach from where you already stand.
examples: The natural adjacency from creator finance content is creator financial tooling — same audience, same trust, different product.
Adjacencies are cheap to enter and easy to overrate; the audience overlaps, the buying behavior often doesn't.
Expand into an adjacency only when the core is boring enough to run itself.
conversation: Jae: What comes after this?
You: The natural adjacency is creator financial tooling. Same audience, same trust, different product.
entries.note: Ask what transfers — audience, trust, distribution, or nothing. Adjacencies that only share a demographic usually aren't adjacent at all.

entries.definition: The gap between early enthusiasts and the mainstream, where products stall because the two groups buy for different reasons.
examples: Our power users love the community; the chasm is everyone who wants to be told what to do and doesn't want a community at all.
Crossing the chasm means abandoning the messaging that got you your first 10,000 users.
Early adopters forgive rough edges as authenticity; the mainstream reads the same edges as risk.
conversation: Maya: Power users love the community feature.
You: The chasm is everyone who wants to be told what to do and does not want a community at all.
entries.note: From Geoffrey Moore. The uncomfortable implication is that your most passionate users are the least representative of the market you need next.

entries.definition: To divide a market into groups that behave differently enough to be worth treating differently.
examples: Segment by what they came for, not by age — “sent here by a creator” and “found us in the App Store” behave like two different products.
A segment you can't reach differently isn't a segment, it's a description.
Over-segmenting produces a plan nobody has the staff to execute.
conversation: Dan: I segmented by age.
You: Segment by what they came for instead. Sent by a creator and found us in the App Store behave like two different products.
entries.note: The test for a real segment: different needs, reachable through a different channel, and big enough to matter. Two out of three is a demographic slide.

entries.definition: The limit that actually governs what's possible right now — the thing you'd have to change to get a different answer.
examples: Our constraint isn't budget, it's my review time; a bigger budget makes the queue longer, not the output better.
Name the binding constraint in the memo's first paragraph and the rest of the argument gets much shorter.
Strategy is mostly choosing which constraint to attack and which to accept for now.
conversation: Jae: If I gave you double the budget?
You: It would not help. The constraint is my review time, not money. Double the budget just makes the queue longer.
entries.note: Sibling of bottleneck, at a strategic altitude. Teams that argue for months are usually arguing about the plan while disagreeing about the constraint.

entries.definition: The set of beliefs an industry accepts without re-examining them.
examples: The orthodoxy in fintech marketing is that trust comes from looking like a bank; our whole thesis is that for this audience it comes from a person.
Every orthodoxy was once an insight that stopped being tested.
The strongest LinkedIn posts name an orthodoxy precisely and then show the counterexample.
conversation: You: The orthodoxy in fintech is that trust comes from looking like a bank.
Jae: And your claim?
You: For this audience it comes from a person. That is the whole thesis in one sentence.
entries.note: A reliable engine for the deep memo: state the orthodoxy in one sentence, show where it came from, then show where it stopped being true.

entries.definition: A modest, welcome offering that gets you inside — and carries the larger ambition with it.
synonyms: way in disguised as something else
examples: The weekly market explainer is a trojan horse: people come for the takes and end up with a funded account.
A trojan horse only works if the first thing is genuinely good on its own terms.
Every successful wedge product is a trojan horse the market let in willingly.
conversation: Dan: Why put so much into a free weekly explainer?
You: It is a trojan horse. They come for the takes and leave with a funded account. It only works because the explainer is genuinely good.
entries.note: The mechanism is consent — the horse gets wheeled in because people want it. If the first offering isn't independently valuable, it's a bait-and-switch and it reads as one.

entries.definition: A change of direction that keeps one foot planted — you hold something (the audience, the insight, the technology) and change everything else.
examples: Moving from paid social to creators was a pivot in channel, not in thesis: same audience, same insight about trust, different distribution.
A pivot that changes the audience and the product isn't a pivot, it's a new company with the old cap table.
The best pivots keep the thing that was working and abandon the thing everyone was emotionally attached to.
conversation: Investor: You pivoted last year?
You: In channel, not in thesis. Same audience, same insight about trust, different distribution. The foot stayed planted.
entries.note: The planted foot is the whole idea, and it's the part most usages drop. Say what stays fixed and the word does real work.

entries.definition: A specific industry or niche served end-to-end, as opposed to a broad tool serving everyone shallowly.
examples: Going vertical on Gen Z finance means we lose the generalist audience and win the ability to say something specific.
Horizontal products win on scale; vertical products win on knowing exactly what the customer's Tuesday looks like.
The vertical is only worth owning if it's growing or nobody's serving it well.
conversation: Jae: Should we broaden out of finance?
You: Going vertical costs us the generalist audience and buys us the right to say something specific. I would keep it.
entries.note: Pairs with horizontal. The strategic trade is always reach versus depth of understanding, and early-stage companies almost always underweight depth.

entries.definition: Describing the advantage claimed by whoever got to a market first.
examples: First-mover advantage is real for about a quarter, and then it's just a head start someone better funded can erase.
We had first-mover advantage on creator-led finance content and mostly spent it learning what didn't work.
First-mover advantage only converts into a moat if you use the time to build something structural.
conversation: Dan: We were first to creator-led finance content.
You: First-mover advantage lasts about a quarter. The question is what we built with the head start.
entries.note: Treat it skeptically in memos — the empirical record favors fast followers. The useful question is what the first mover did with the head start.

entries.definition: Cost advantages that arrive because you're bigger — the per-unit cost falls as volume rises.
examples: There are real economies of scale in creator ops: the 40th brief costs a fraction of the 4th because the template already exists.
Creative doesn't have economies of scale the way media buying does — every video still needs a person with taste.
Claiming economies of scale means claiming a specific cost that falls; name it or don't claim it.
conversation: Jae: Does the fortieth creator cost the same as the fourth?
You: No, and that is the economies of scale. The template exists now. The creative still needs a person with taste.
entries.note: In creator and content businesses, look for economies of scale in process and casting, not in the creative itself. That's where the actual leverage hides.

entries.definition: The means by which a product reaches people — the channels, relationships, and surfaces that put it in front of them.
examples: We have distribution and a product gap, which is a much better problem than the reverse.
Distribution is the scarce asset in this market; anyone can ship an investing app in a quarter.
Design for the distribution you have, not the one in the case study.
conversation: Investor: What is scarce in this market?
You: Distribution. Anyone can ship an investing app in a quarter. Nobody can ship forty million monthly views.
entries.note: The central asset in Jun's job. Frame the creator program as a distribution asset rather than a marketing expense, and the budget conversation changes shape.

entries.definition: To sell several things together as one offer, at one price.
examples: We bundle the lessons with the brokerage because separately, nobody would pay for the lessons and nobody would trust the brokerage.
Bundling hides the price of the weak item and raises the value of the strong one.
A bundle is a positioning decision before it's a pricing decision.
conversation: Dan: Should the lessons be a separate paid tier?
You: We bundle them. Separately nobody pays for lessons and nobody trusts a new brokerage.
entries.note: Bundling and unbundling alternate in every market. Knowing which phase you're in tells you whether to add or to strip.

entries.definition: To pull one valuable piece out of an existing package and offer it alone, better.
examples: Creators unbundled financial media from financial institutions — the advice left the building and the accounts followed.
Every fintech of the last decade unbundled one line item off a bank statement.
Unbundling wins on focus and then slowly rebundles to survive.
conversation: Jae: What is the one-line origin story?
You: Creators unbundled financial media from financial institutions. The advice left the building and the accounts followed.
entries.note: The Bloom origin story in one word. Worth saying out loud in a memo: what did we unbundle, and what will we have to rebundle to keep the customer?

entries.definition: To set a reference point that shapes how everything after it is judged.
examples: The first number in the deck anchors the whole conversation — lead with 40M views and $12 CAC sounds cheap.
Anchor the price against a $200 advisor session, not against a free app.
Whoever states the first number is doing the anchoring, whether or not they intended to.
conversation: Maya: Which number goes on slide one?
You: Whichever one anchors the rest. Lead with forty million views and twelve dollar CAC sounds cheap.
entries.note: A cognitive bias you can use ethically by choosing an honest, relevant comparison — and one you should notice being used on you in every negotiation.

entries.definition: Describing an entrant that starts out worse on the metrics incumbents care about, serves an overlooked segment, and improves until it takes the market.
examples: A 60-second creator video is disruptive in the strict sense: worse than a financial advisor on every traditional axis, and it reaches people the advisor never would.
Most things called disruptive are just competitive — better products attacking the same customers head-on.
The incumbent's rational response to a disruptive entrant is to ignore it, which is exactly why it works.
conversation: Dan: Everyone calls their product disruptive.
You: Most of it is just competitive. A sixty-second creator video is genuinely disruptive — worse than an advisor on every traditional axis, and it reaches people the advisor never would.
entries.note: Christensen's technical meaning, and the misuse is now so common that using it correctly is itself a signal. Say “new” or “better” when that's what you mean.

entries.definition: To skip a stage of development entirely and land ahead of where the incumbent stands.
examples: This audience leapfrogged the bank branch and the robo-advisor; their first financial relationship is a person on a screen.
Emerging markets leapfrogged desktop banking straight to mobile wallets.
You can't leapfrog by copying the leader's roadmap faster.
conversation: Jae: Why do none of these users have a broker relationship?
You: They leapfrogged it. Their first financial relationship is a person on a screen.
entries.note: Best used about customer behavior rather than about your own product. Claiming your company leapfrogged someone rarely lands; showing that users skipped a step always does.

entries.definition: A concrete piece of evidence that makes a claim believable rather than aspirational.
examples: The claim is that creators build trust; the proof point is that creator-sourced users fund accounts at 2.3× the rate of paid-social users.
Every value theme in the positioning doc needs a proof point, or it's a promise.
One specific number beats three adjectives as a proof point.
conversation: Investor: You say creators build trust. Prove it.
You: Proof point: creator-sourced users fund accounts at 2.3 times the rate of paid-social users.
entries.note: From April Dunford's positioning canvas. When a message isn't landing, it's usually missing a proof point, not missing enthusiasm.
